title: Apaitu mṛtyuḥ: let death go away
theme: The first of six verses that turn death away: death is to depart, the deathless to come, Yama to grant fearlessness, harm to fall away like a ripe leaf and wealth to stay.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «मृत्युरस्मत्तोऽपैतु दूरी भूयात्» — may death go away from us, be far off
The anonymous commentator: amṛta here is liberation: «मोक्ष आगन्नागच्छतु»
The commentator renders it as a wish (āgacchatu, ‘may it come’).
The anonymous commentator: «वैवस्वतो यमो नोऽस्मभ्यमभयं नारकदुःखाभावं कृणोतु करोतु» — Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is to make for us fearlessness, the absence of the sufferings of hell

words.role: main verb of the second clause

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «वनस्पतेरश्वत्थादेः पक्कपर्णमिवाभिशीयतामभितो विशीर्य नश्यतु» — like the ripe leaf of a tree such as the aśvattha, may it fall away on every side and perish

words.meaning: of a tree (lit. lord of the forest)

words.role: connects the falling-away with the speakers
words.context: The verse names no subject for śīyatām; the commentator supplies our sin: «नोऽस्मदीयं पापं».
The anonymous commentator: «महदैश्वर्यं सचतां प्राप्नोतु» — great prosperity; may it reach us

words.meaning: lord of Śacī (Indra); lord of might
words.context: The anonymous commentator: he takes it as describing the wealth: «इन्द्रोपभोग्य इत्यर्थः» — such as Indra enjoys

sandhi.type: a + e → ai with a preverb before eti
sandhi.rule: apa + etu → apaitu: vṛddhi, not the pararūpa a preverb otherwise takes (P. 6.1.89 (एत्येधत्यूठ्सु)).

sandhi.type: visarga after u before a vowel
sandhi.rule: The visarga of mṛtyuḥ becomes r before a vowel.

sandhi.type: -aḥ before a vowel other than a; -aḥ before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: naḥ + āgan → na āgan, the visarga dropped (P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)); vaivasvataḥ + naḥ → vaivasvato naḥ (P. 6.1.114 (हशि च)).

sandhi.type: m before a consonant; visarga after e; a + a
sandhi.rule: parṇam → parṇaṃ (P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः)); vanaspateḥ + iva → vanaspater iva; iva + abhi → ivābhi (P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः)).
The recitation text writes the visarga before s as s (P. 8.3.36 (वा शरि) allows either); the other two witnesses write ः स (spelling only).

sandhi_exceptions.note: naḥ · abhayam: -aḥ before a written -o with the a kept (classical no ’bhayam); a Vedic hiatus, printed so in every witness.

samasa.meaning: lord of Śacī, or lord of might
lord of the forest, a tree

morphology.note: A root aorist of √gam with ā (ā-agam-t, the t lost after m, and m → n at the end of a word). The commentator renders it as a wish.
√śad ‘to fall off’ makes its present stem śīya- (śīyate ‘falls away’); here the middle imperative.
The anonymous bhāṣya as printed reads नयिः (नोऽस्मान्नयिर्महदैश्वर्यं), a misprint for रयिः; it then asks «रयिः कीदृशः।».

translation.literal: Let death go away; immortality has come to us; may the son of Vivasvat make fearlessness for us. Like the leaf of a tree, let [it] fall away from us on every side; may wealth attend us, the lord of Śacī.
translation.readable: May death go far from us and the deathless come to us; may Yama, the son of Vivasvat, give us freedom from fear. Like a ripe leaf from a tree, may what harms us fall away on every side; may wealth, such as Indra enjoys, stay with us.

anvaya: मृत्युः अपैतु । अमृतम् नः आगन् । वैवस्वतः नः अभयम् कृणोतु । वनस्पतेः पर्णम् इव नः [पापम्] अभि शीयताम् । शचीपतिः रयिः नः सचताम् ।
syntax: Five short wishes in the imperative (apaitu, kṛṇotu, śīyatām, sacatām) and one aorist (āgan) read as a wish. The fourth clause has no subject in the verse; the commentator supplies pāpam, our sin.

ambiguities.note: The verse says only ‘let [it] fall away from us like a leaf’. The commentator supplies our sin; read with the first line, death itself could be meant.
The commentator takes the word as describing the wealth, ‘such as Indra enjoys’. Read on its own it is a nominative, and may be a second subject: ‘may wealth, may the lord of might, be with us’.
Grammatically ‘has come’; the commentator reads it as a wish, ‘may it come’ (āgacchatu).

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: One triṣṭubh verse (four pādas of 11) printed in two lines; the checker counts 22 and 23 syllables, the extra one in the second line from reading rayis sacatāṃ with its doubled s.

beginner: This is the first of a short group of verses that ask death to go away. It makes five wishes, one after another. Death should leave; the deathless, which the old commentator explains as liberation, should come; Yama, the god who rules over the dead and is called the son of Vivasvat, should grant freedom from fear. Then comes a picture from nature: like a ripe leaf that drops from a tree, may harm fall away from us on every side. The commentator says that what falls away is our sin. Last, the verse asks that wealth stay with the speakers. The commentator reads the final word, lord of Śacī, a name of Indra, as describing that wealth: the kind of prosperity a king of the gods enjoys.
analogy: Like an autumn tree letting go of its dry leaves: they are not torn off, they simply fall away.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That death depart, the deathless come, Yama grant fearlessness, harm fall away like a leaf, and wealth remain.

commentary.q: How does the commentator read it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: with this verse the speaker asks the Lord for what he desires («अनयर्चा परमात्मनः सकाशात्स्वाभीष्टं याचते»); amṛta is liberation, Yama’s gift of fearlessness is the absence of the sufferings of hell, and what falls like a ripe leaf is our sin.

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: The movement from death to the deathless is the prayer of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.3.28), ‘from death lead me to the deathless’: «मृत्योर्मामृतं».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this verse is in the edition’s sources. Only the anonymous commentator comments on it, and his reading is a prayer to the Lord (paramātman) without a school argument; Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s files contain no comment on this verse, and Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

parallels.note: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka’s prayer ‘lead me from death to the deathless’ makes the same movement as the first line here.

contemporary.text: The image of the ripe leaf asks for no struggle: what is finished simply drops. Many people find that what they fear loosens when it is named and let go rather than fought. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What in your life is like a ripe leaf, ready to fall?
reflect.deeper: Why might a prayer against death begin by asking for fearlessness rather than for long life?
reflect.practice: Name one worry you have carried too long, and decide one small way to set it down this week.

references.text: Only the anonymous commentator comments on this anuvāka; the edition’s Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara files have no comment on it (the concordance maps are empty here, correctly).

flags.note: The subject of śīyatām (pāpam, ‘our sin’) is supplied from the commentary, not the verse; it is marked [supplied] in the anvaya.
